The Board

The Money Keeping Ukraine in the War

Russia is claiming villages its army has not reached, and Berlin is deciding this week whether Ukraine's factories get the money to keep that true. A financing gap, a span in the water, a governor's signature in Belgorod and a front that went backwards are one story told at four ranges: the money, what the money buys, and the ground the money holds.

Scroll

The Front

The spool is the weapon.

A Ukrainian soldier holds a fiber-optic drone and the spool of cable that guides it, immune to jamming. This is the weapon that froze the front, and it is made in factories that can build three times what Ukraine can afford to buy.

Photograph by ArmyInform, via Wikimedia Commons. A fiber-optic drone in a soldier’s hands. The cable unspools behind the drone in flight, carrying the pilot’s signal where radio jamming cannot reach it.

What’s Moved

Ukraine struck the Kerch Strait Bridge for the second straight night and dropped its road arch, two days before Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sit down in Shenzhen. Russia answered on Kyiv’s bridges and left 700,000 families in one province without power.

In Berlin on Thursday, more than twenty governments meet over a financing gap for Ukraine that the International Monetary Fund puts at $32 billion to $34 billion for 2027 alone. Beyond the war, the week’s other paper moved the same way and is tracked in the watchlist: in Washington, the Federal Reserve’s October meeting minutes land Wednesday ahead of a December vote the futures market has priced as a certainty its own formula manufactures, and in Texas, state regulators issued eight power plant permits on Monday while a queue of 474 gigawatts of proposed data centers narrows to 17 loads that have cleared every gate but the last.

Verdict

This week’s loudest numbers are paper. Russia’s defence ministry claims villages 18 to 27 kilometres beyond the line its own army has reached. Berlin’s announced totals blur money approved, money transferred and money locked for a later year into a single figure that sounds like a decision. Shenzhen will produce a photograph of three presidents, and a photograph binds nothing.

Underneath the paper, the facts with mass are narrower and harder, and they form a chain. The front in Ukraine lost Russia ground in October. A bridge span is in the water. Ukraine’s factories can build two or three times the drones its budget can buy, and Russia’s liquid savings fund holds $44.4 billion against a war budget that grows by a quarter next year, with governors already cutting the payments at both ends of the recruitment ledger.

The decisions that will bind are the ones being signed this week in Berlin’s financing rooms and Beijing’s export licensing offices, not the ones being announced. Berlin’s money decides what Ukraine’s factories build. What the factories build decides what the front can hold. The map is the last page of that ledger, not the first.

Chapter One

Berlin Counts

Thursday's other meeting has no photograph worth taking. It has a gap of $32 billion to $34 billion, and the people in the room are the ones who have to appropriate it.

On Thursday, while Trump, Xi and Putin sit down in Shenzhen, more than twenty governments meet in Berlin in the Coalition of the Willing format, with Chancellor Merz, President Macron and Prime Minister Burnham at the head of the table. Putin arrives in Shenzhen selling the map his officers tabled in Abu Dhabi. Trump arrives wanting a settlement he can announce. Xi arrives wanting to leave Shenzhen with his leverage exactly as he brought it in: the indispensable host, the one man in the room whose country’s factories are feeding the war the other two are there to discuss, and whose export licences are the one supply decision neither of them can make for him. Thursday’s other meeting gets the photograph. Berlin gets the ledger.

History offers no comfort about what summit formats settle. No meeting of American, Chinese and Russian leaders as a trio exists in the record to copy. Yalta in 1945 worked, to the extent it did, because the three men in the room were wartime allies whose armies already held the ground being divided. In Shenzhen, one of the three is arming a fourth country that is not invited, and the ground being discussed is held by the country left outside. The 1972 opening to China, the closest American precedent for a triangular move, took seven months of secret preparation and still produced a formula rather than a settlement. Formats decide who may speak. They do not decide who can pay, produce or hold.

Two letters are already sitting on the desk of António Costa, the European Council president in whose rooms the money must eventually be voted. On November 5, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni wrote demanding the Union decide once and for all who sits at the negotiating table for Europe, and with what mandate. She asked for no seat for Italy. What she refused was commitments negotiated without a mandate that Italy would then be bound by. In a letter dated November 6, Germany’s Friedrich Merz wrote with a harder instrument: Germany’s backing for the European Union’s next seven year budget is conditional on every member state, without exception, helping to close Ukraine’s financing gap. The budget needs every government’s vote, which makes the condition a veto with a price attached. Slovakia’s Robert Fico called it blackmail. Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria have all signalled they will not pay.

The third party in the room is not in the room. China is the war’s decisive enabler, and its contribution is also measured in physical flows. Chinese dual use exports to Russia, goods with civilian and military uses, have run at roughly $525 million a month since the invasion. Investigators who have taken apart recovered Geran drones find Chinese parts making up 60 to 65 percent of the electronics. In the first quarter of 2025, 87 percent of Russia’s chemical imports came from China. Beijing announced new dual use export controls on October 19. They take effect on November 18, this week, the day before Shenzhen. Whether those controls are a valve being closed or a valve being priced is the most consequential unknown in the war economy, and it will be answered by shipping data, not by anything said on Thursday. Merz’s Berlin arithmetic quietly depends on that answer. If the flow bends, the factories Berlin is trying to outspend lose their cheapest inputs; if it does not, his condition buys time against an opponent whose supply lines run through the room next door.

The ledger is specific. The International Monetary Fund’s programme for Ukraine leaves a residual financing gap, money Kyiv needs and does not yet have committed, of $32 billion to $34 billion in 2027 and about $17 billion in 2028. That residual is the sum Merz’s condition is meant to force his partners to cover, and the sum Meloni’s mandate fight is meant to govern: money no programme has yet committed, argued over by people who have not yet voted it. That gap is the distance between factories idled for want of orders and factories running full, between power rationed through the winter and power that holds, between a front that holds and a front that thins. European governments have spent two years announcing totals that blur three different things, money approved, money transferred and money locked for a later year. Berlin is where the 2027 half gets argued over by the people who have to appropriate it.

Chapter Two

The Burn

Attrition is a purchasing problem. Russia pays two and a half times more for a recruit than it did two years ago; Ukraine's factories outrun its budget by a factor of three.

Zelensky said plainly on October 16 what Berlin’s uncommitted gap looks like from Kyiv: Ukraine could produce two or three times more drones and simply does not have the money. His drone industry can produce more than 8 million first person view drones a year, the small camera guided drones a pilot flies into a target through a video feed, spread across more than 160 firms. The state can afford to buy only part of it: public procurement uses roughly 30 percent of Ukraine’s defence-industrial capacity, an EU estimate finds. The factories are not the bottleneck. The budget is. Russia’s constraint runs the other way, and it starts with what Russia fires.

Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service estimates Russia produced about 7 million large calibre rounds in 2025, howitzer, mortar, tank and rocket artillery together, up from about 400,000 in 2021. That figure is often misquoted as shells comparable to NATO’s 155 millimetre production. It is not the same category, and the comparison flatters whoever makes it. North Korea fills much of the remaining gap. Ukrainian military intelligence estimates Pyongyang supplies a quarter to two fifths of Russia’s artillery ammunition, and assessed North Korean rounds at roughly half of Russian front line expenditure in the second half of 2025.

Men are the harder input. Russia recruits about 30,000 contract soldiers a month. The rate is not a Kremlin statement. The analyst Janis Kluge derives it from the signing bonuses sitting in regional budgets: every contract a man signs leaves a bonus payment behind it in some region’s accounts, and Kluge counts the payments. It is the war’s manpower ledger, kept in the open, one payment at a time. The price of a recruit tells the tighter story. An effective contract in the regions where men actually sign now costs about 3.4 million roubles up front, two and a half times the price of two years ago. In October, on Ukrainian loss figures adjusted for the share assessed as permanent, Russia’s irreversible losses ran about 31,600 against those 30,000 recruits. The month the replacement line crossed is a month built on one side’s loss claims, and it should be read as an estimate, not a count. The direction is corroborated by the price. Armies do not pay two and a half times more for a man they can easily get.

The money behind the price is thinning at the edges. Russia’s National Wealth Fund, the sovereign savings pot built from past oil revenue, held $44.4 billion in liquid assets on November 1, about 1.5 percent of the country’s output. Oil and gas revenue fell 17.2 percent in the first nine months of 2026. The planned defence budget for 2027 is 17.1 trillion roubles, 27 percent above the figure originally budgeted. The fund does not pay for the war by itself, and Russia can still borrow at home. But a savings buffer of $44.4 billion against a defence plan growing by a quarter is a shrinking cushion, and everyone in the Berlin meeting on Thursday can do that arithmetic.

In Belgorod, the arithmetic has a name and a signature on it. On October 30, Governor Alexander Shuvaev cut the payment his region makes to the family of a soldier killed in Ukraine from 3 million roubles to 1 million. Belgorod is a border region that buries men from the same regiments the signing bonuses recruit into. The decision is the war’s ledger kept at both ends by the same hands: pay more to fill the ranks at the front of the book, pay less to close them at the back.

The economics of the air war show why the money matters at that scale. A Ukrainian interceptor drone costs $1,000 to $2,500. The Geran it hunts costs about $35,000. A Patriot class interceptor, the kind that stops ballistic missiles, is produced in the United States at roughly 40 to 60 a month and priced in millions. Ukraine’s answer is a layered defence where the cheap weapon takes the cheap target, and it works only while production runs ahead of Russia’s jet drone output, now estimated at 3,000 to 4,000 a month. Every element of that sentence is a factory and a budget line, not a battlefield event. The war’s decisive production decisions are being made by purchasing departments.

Chapter Three

Two Nights Over the Strait

Ukraine did not raid the Kerch Bridge this time. It ran a campaign against the defences first, then dropped the span, then hit the only other road into Crimea the same night.

The production race is not an abstraction, and this week its scoreboard was a bridge. On the second night, the arch went down. Geolocated imagery assessed by the Institute for the Study of War, ISW, shows the Kerch Strait Bridge’s automobile span collapsed into the strait on the night of November 16 into 17, the railway section damaged beside it. Russian transport authorities suspended traffic, then reopened a single rail track. By morning the bridge that supplies Crimea was a one-track railway and a gap.

The bridge has been attacked before, by a truck bomb in 2022, by naval drones in 2023, by an underwater charge in 2025. Each time it was damaged and repaired. This week Ukraine came back with a campaign instead of a device. For weeks, by President Zelensky’s account on Tuesday, Ukrainian forces worked through seven stages against Crimea’s air defences, radars and electronic warfare systems, the radars and jammers that exist to blind exactly this kind of attack. On the night of November 15 into 16 they struck the bridge. On the night of November 16 into 17 they struck it again. The road section took Palianytsia drones, jet powered strike drones built in Ukraine. The rail section took Neptune, Ruta and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, the Flamingo a Ukrainian built missile from a company called Fire Point, flown with a live video feed to the moment of impact.

A collapsed span is a fact with mass. It does not need a communiqué. Crimea is supplied by two land arteries, the bridge and the M-14 highway running from Rostov along the coast. Ukraine struck the highway the same night, at the bridge over the Mius River. Whatever Russia now moves into Crimea moves slower, on one road, under observation.

Russia answered in the same grammar. Ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges. A jet powered Geran drone, Russia’s version of the Iranian designed Shahed, hit the Preobrazhensky Bridge in Zaporizhzhia city. Overnight on November 16 into 17, Ukraine’s air force counted 306 Russian drones and loitering munitions launched, 92 of them jet powered, with direct impacts recorded in 44 locations. By morning, DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private power company, counted 700,000 families without electricity in Dnipropetrovsk province alone, with outages across eight more provinces and emergency cutoffs in two others.

That exchange is the war’s real centre of gravity this winter, and it is not the front line. Since October 2025, Russian strikes have damaged about 8.5 gigawatts of Ukrainian generating capacity. Ukraine goes into the coldest weeks with roughly 11 gigawatts available against demand that reaches about 18 gigawatts at winter’s hardest. The gap is closed, or not, by air defence interceptors and repair crews, and both of those are bought with money allocated in rooms far from the front. Which is why the strike on the bridge and the meeting in Berlin on Thursday are the same story told at two ranges.

Ukraine’s deep strike campaign runs the other direction as well. Since the start of October, Ukrainian drones have hit at least 13 Russian refineries. Two industry sources, speaking to Reuters and carried in ISW’s reporting, estimate the strikes have cut Russian refining capacity by about 30 percent, from roughly 930,000 tons a day to about 700,000. Rosneft has reintroduced purchase limits at its Moscow stations, 50 litres per vehicle. The country that exports oil is rationing petrol at home while its army advances a third of a square kilometre a day.

Chapter Four

The Map and the Ground

Russia is selling a front line in Abu Dhabi and Shenzhen that its own army has not reached. The assessed line is narrower, and it is moving the wrong way.

All of it, the money, the factories and the strikes, is finally audited in one place: the ground. On the night of November 10 in Abu Dhabi, Russian officers told American and Ukrainian delegations that Russia already held half of the Ukrainian-held Donbas. It was a negotiating move dressed as a map. The Institute for the Study of War, which tracks the front from geolocated footage, calls the Russian presentation a carefully crafted fictional version of the front line, built to set the starting line for talks.

The actual line tells a different story. In October, Russian forces seized or consolidated 139.85 square kilometres of Ukraine and lost 167.14. The month’s net was a Russian loss of 27.29 square kilometres, the second straight month Russia went backwards. Its claims have gone the other way. The defence ministry in Moscow claimed 38 settlements taken in October. In November it has claimed villages at Vasylkove, Voskresenka and Tersianka that sit 18 to 27 kilometres beyond the nearest ground ISW can confirm Russian troops have reached. Infiltration errors in geolocation are measured in hundreds of metres. A gap of 27 kilometres is not an error. It is a product.

The ground war underneath those claims is a war of small groups moving through a transparent battlefield. Drones watch nearly everything within 15 to 30 kilometres of the line, so armour masses only to die. Infantry goes forward in ones and twos. In the Kupyansk sector this week, a Ukrainian spokesman reported that Russian infiltration groups northwest of the town had thinned to individuals, worn down by losses. Russia’s own assault pattern in the south has thinned the same way, single infiltrators replacing two and three man teams, even as the number of assaults rose.

The sectors have names and owners, and they matter more than the arrows on a briefing map. Around Dobropillya, Russia’s 51st Combined Arms Army of the Central Grouping of Forces is making the army’s main effort, some 30 attacks a day through the start of November, the highest tempo since August, aimed at encircling Ukraine’s Fortress Belt from the southwest. It has not consolidated ground in Dobropillya itself. At Kostyantynivka, the 8th Combined Arms Army has been infiltrating since October 2025. ISW assesses Russian troops have advanced into about 36 percent of the town. Ukrainian positions remain inside it, at least 41 of them observed since September 1. The town is the southern gate of the Fortress Belt, the chain of fortified cities running through Druzhkivka, Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. Russia claimed Kostyantynivka in July. It is still fighting for the first third of it.

Ukraine’s largest success of the year came on the belt’s other flank. The 3rd Army Corps, built by Andrii Biletskyi, the founder of the Azov movement who now commands Ukraine’s Center Grouping of Forces, ran an operation ISW calls Vivaldi through the summer and autumn toward Lyman. Before any ground assault, the corps spent months striking Russian logistics, fuel and drone operators at intermediate range. ISW assessed at least 147 square kilometres retaken. A Russian motor rifle division on that axis effectively ceased to exist as an organised force, by Ukrainian accounts carried in ISW’s reporting. The northern pincer that was supposed to close on the Fortress Belt from above the Siverskyi Donets river is, in ISW’s assessment, operationally defeated.

Add the year’s shape and the stall is plain. Russia took 3,604 square kilometres in 2024 and about 4,831 in Ukraine proper in 2025. Across the first ten months of 2026 it has taken 117. Its daily rate of advance has fallen from 13.25 square kilometres in 2025 to 0.38 this year. Ukraine, meanwhile, retook more than 745 square kilometres across three provinces in the winter and spring, its first sustained gains since the Kursk operation of 2024.

The cost of that arithmetic is counted two honest ways and one dishonest one. Mediazona and the BBC, working name by name through obituaries and official notices, had confirmed 285,023 Russian dead by October 30. That is a floor, not a total, because it counts only the named. A Ukrainian project, UALosses, had recorded 106,285 named Ukrainian dead by late October, with a similar number listed missing. The dishonest way is the claimant’s tally, and both general staffs publish one daily. Neither prints here. The bill returns to the budgets that opened this report: every name on those two lists is a payment a region must make, at the price its governor has just cut, or a factory shift a budget in Berlin has not yet funded.

Chapter Five

Two Rival Reads

Does the chain decide while the paper makes noise, or is the paper itself the settlement being written? Two coherent answers, and the tests that separate them.

Read One: the chain decides, and the paper is noise. On this read, the week is simpler than it looks. The front is frozen because both armies have hit their replacement limits at current budgets, and the war’s outcome now runs through the chain this report follows: Berlin’s appropriations for 2027, the factories those appropriations keep running, Beijing’s licensing of the dual use flow that feeds the other side’s factories, and the ground that records the result. Shenzhen produces a photograph because none of the three men in the room can bind the others, and each is buying time. What would prove this read: Berlin closes most of the 2027 gap with appropriated money rather than pledges, Ukrainian procurement rises toward the capacity its factories already have, Chinese export data for December shows the new controls biting into the $525 million monthly flow, and the front’s monthly net stays at or below zero through winter. What would kill it: a Shenzhen text with enforcement language on Ukraine, or a Russian ground offensive that takes real ground before spring, either of which would mean the rooms and the claims still outrank the ledgers.

Read Two: the paper is the early form of the settlement, and it is being written now. On this read, inflated claims are not noise around the process. They are the process. Russia’s fictional map is a bid, tabled in Abu Dhabi and carried into Shenzhen, asking to be paid for ground it has not taken because paying is cheaper for everyone else than another year of war. Berlin’s announced totals do similar work, letting governments claim the gap is handled while the appropriations that would actually handle it wait for a vote. What would prove this read: a Shenzhen or post Shenzhen text that adopts language from the Abu Dhabi presentation, or a Berlin closing statement that presents a pledge total as the answer to the 2027 gap and is accepted as one. What would kill it: Berlin funding the gap with appropriated money in full, and Shenzhen producing no text at all or one that restates the assessed line, which would show the claims were only ever claims.

Chapter Six

Scenarios

Four ways the board moves from here, each with the evidence that would confirm it and the evidence that would kill it.

Scenario One: the ledgers close, the front stays frozen. Berlin appropriates most of Ukraine’s 2027 gap, China’s controls trim the dual use flow, and Russia’s advance stays under a square kilometre a day through winter. The war becomes a contest of budgets with a fixed map. Confirming trigger: a Berlin closing statement carrying a specific appropriated figure for 2027, not a pledge total. Killing trigger: December export data showing Chinese dual use shipments to Russia unchanged.

Scenario Two: the map gets paid for. A text emerges from Shenzhen or the weeks after it that trades Ukrainian territory Russia has not taken for sanctions relief or a ceasefire in place, using the Abu Dhabi presentation as its factual basis. Confirming trigger: any joint or American statement describing Russian control in the Donbas in terms closer to Moscow’s claimed half than to ISW’s assessed line. Killing trigger: a public American or European restatement of the assessed line as the basis for talks, or Ukraine striking the M-14 corridor hard enough to force a visible Russian logistics crisis in Crimea.

Scenario Three: the valve closes. Beijing’s controls, in force from November 18, bite into the electronics flow, Geran production slows for want of Chinese parts, and Russia’s strike tempo falls through the winter. Confirming trigger: December and January export data showing the monthly dual use flow down materially, with the jet powered share of Russia’s nightly drone counts falling with it. Killing trigger: the flow holding at roughly $525 million a month and jet drone output staying at 3,000 to 4,000 a month.

Scenario Four: the burn outruns the budget. More Russian regions follow Belgorod’s governor and cut payments at one or both ends of the ledger, recruitment falls short of losses for a second straight month, and Moscow faces the choice it has spent two years avoiding: a mobilisation it does not want, or an offensive tempo it cannot sustain. On the other side of the same scenario, Berlin’s gap stays open and Ukraine’s factories idle for want of orders while the front thins. Confirming trigger: further regional payment decrees through December, with Kluge’s bonus count showing recruitment below the loss line again. Killing trigger: recruitment holding at about 30,000 a month at stable prices, or Berlin appropriating the gap in full.

Chapter Seven

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

Berlin, Thursday. A specific appropriated figure for Ukraine’s 2027 gap, against the $32 billion to $34 billion the IMF leaves open. A pledge total instead of an appropriation means the gap survives the meeting, and the factories idle with it.

Shenzhen, Thursday. Any written text at all, and if one appears, whether its description of the war matches the assessed front or the claimed one. The format is the tell.

Chinese export data for November and December. The dual use controls took effect November 18. The monthly flow, running at roughly $525 million, either bends or it does not.

The payment decrees and the monthly net. More regions cutting signing or death payments would confirm the burn is outrunning regional budgets; the front’s November net, after two months of Russian losses, shows whether the stall is holding.

Beyond the war, in one line each. The Fed: October minutes Wednesday, the October core PCE reading November 25, the November jobs report December 4, the vote December 9, four documents that decide whether a manufactured certainty becomes a real one. Texas: the December 10 filings by ERCOT, the nonprofit that runs the state grid, and the December 17 commission meeting decide which of the 474 paper gigawatts become real obligations.
